persona.name: Maya
persona.context: Shares an apartment, studies mainly at home, and has afternoon classes.
constraints: must finish the degree this term
fact_ledger: She postpones studying until late evening.
Notifications usually start a long social-media break.
She studies reliably at the library with a friend.
Avoidance creates guilt and worsens her sleep.

initial_problem: I keep putting off studying even though finals are close. I end up scrolling until midnight, feel guilty, and then sleep badly. I want to study consistently without panicking every night.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What usually happens right before you start scrolling?
rephrase_cases.context: She has discussed where she studies but not what precedes scrolling.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What usually happens right before you start scrolling?
rephrase_cases.context: She said a notification arrives and she opens the app automatically.

rephrase_cases.original_question: How does your phone affect studying?
rephrase_cases.context: She said daytime phone use is manageable but late-night scrolling keeps displacing revision.

conversation.content: What usually happens right before you start scrolling?
A notification pops up while I am reading, and I tap it without really deciding to.
What usually happens right before you start scrolling?
I don't know, life is just hard.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: Can you think of the last time you picked up your phone while studying?

summary_conversation.content: Walk me through the last time your phone interrupted studying.
A group notification appeared around 9 p.m. I meant to check it for a minute, but I kept scrolling for almost two hours and went to bed guilty.
When is it easier to stay off the phone?
At the library with my friend because my phone stays in my bag.

context.document: A notification during evening reading led to nearly two hours of scrolling and guilt.
On three recent home-study nights, checking one message turned into prolonged scrolling.
At the library with a friend, the phone remains in her bag and she completes planned work.
Late scrolling delays sleep and leaves her tired the next morning.

supported_patterns.mechanism: notification to scrolling to guilt and sleep loss
external structure and phone distance protect focus

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Maya
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: Academic procrastination driven by late-night scrolling.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 21-year-old final-year student who focuses better at the library with a friend.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Reduce notification cues, place the phone out of reach, and anchor a small study block to library or friend-supported structure.

persona.name: Jon
persona.context: Works from a bedroom desk and cares for two children after school.
fact_ledger: Back-to-back meetings leave no transition time.
He continues checking work messages during family time.
A protected lunch walk improves afternoon energy.
He wants boundaries rather than a new career.

problem_framing.acceptable_followup: What would you most like to change about how work is affecting you?
problem_framing.clarification_answer: I want to stop carrying work into family time and have enough energy to be present with my kids; I am not looking to quit.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What does the stretch of meetings before childcare usually look like?
rephrase_cases.context: He has not described the meeting schedule.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What does the stretch of meetings before childcare usually look like?
rephrase_cases.context: He described meetings from noon to 3:30 with no break.

rephrase_cases.original_question: How does remote work affect you?
rephrase_cases.context: He said mornings are manageable; the hard transition is from the final meeting directly into childcare.

conversation.content: What is the end of your workday usually like?
My last call ends at 3:30 exactly when the children get home, so I close the laptop already tense.
What is the end of your workday usually like?
Whatever.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: What tends to be happening as you finish work?

summary_conversation.content: Walk me through the end of a typical workday.
Meetings run until 3:30, then the kids arrive. There is no pause, and I keep checking Slack while helping with homework.
When does the afternoon go better?
If I protect lunch for a short walk, I am less drained later.

context.document: Meetings repeatedly end exactly when childcare begins, leaving no transition.
He checks Slack during family tasks on most weekdays and remains mentally at work.
On days with a protected lunch walk, afternoon energy and patience improve.
Back-to-back calls prevent meals or short resets several times a week.

supported_patterns.mechanism: work cues extend stress while a midday reset interrupts it

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Jon
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: Remote-work burnout spills directly into family time.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 38-year-old project manager and parent with no buffer before childcare.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Protect a short midday reset, create a brief work-closing ritual before 3:30, and silence work notifications during family time.

persona.name: Elena
persona.context: Income varies monthly and she works alone from home.
fact_ledger: She avoids opening invoices when income is low.
Avoidance temporarily reduces fear but leads to late fees.
A weekly coworking call helps her handle admin.
One unexpected car repair occurred only once.

initial_problem: Money stuff is a mess and I just can't deal with it lately. It matters because fees keep appearing, but I don't even know where to start.

rephrase_cases.original_question: Can you walk me through the last time you opened an overdue invoice?
rephrase_cases.context: No invoice-opening experience has been discussed.

rephrase_cases.original_question: Can you walk me through the last time you opened an overdue invoice?
rephrase_cases.context: She said she waited ten days, then opened it after a coworking call began.

rephrase_cases.original_question: How do finances affect your routine?
rephrase_cases.context: She handles routine purchases but avoids business invoices specifically in low-income weeks.

conversation.content: What happens when an invoice arrives in a low-income week?
I leave the email unopened because seeing the amount makes the shortage feel real.
What happens when an invoice arrives in a low-income week?
The weather has been strange.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: What do you usually do with the invoice email when it arrives?

summary_conversation.content: Tell me about a recent invoice you avoided.
I left it unopened for ten days because work was slow. That calmed me briefly, but a late fee was added.
When is admin easier?
During a Friday coworking call; having someone else working nearby gets me started.

context.document: During three low-income months, invoices remained unopened until a fee or reminder arrived.
Avoiding the inbox briefly reduces fear but later increases cost and stress.
Weekly coworking calls have repeatedly helped her begin invoicing and payment tasks.
A car repair caused one unusually expensive month.

supported_patterns.mechanism: avoidance gives short relief and creates later fees
social structure helps initiate avoided admin

forbidden_patterns: Car repairs are the recurring cause

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Elena
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: Financial stress drives invoice avoidance and late fees.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 29-year-old freelancer with irregular income who starts admin more easily during coworking.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Use a free weekly coworking block to open and triage invoices in very small steps before avoidance creates fees.

persona.name: Darius
persona.context: Lives alone and no longer sees coworkers daily.
fact_ledger: Retirement removed routine contact.
He skips community events when they start after dark.
A neighbor's Tuesday coffee invitation reliably improves his mood.
He does not want online-only social groups.

initial_problem: Since retiring, the days feel empty and I can go a whole week without a proper conversation. I want more regular contact, but most suggestions seem to involve apps or driving at night.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What was the last community activity you considered attending?
rephrase_cases.context: No specific activity has been discussed.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What was the last community activity you considered attending?
rephrase_cases.context: He considered a workshop but it ended after dark, so he stayed home.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What makes social contact easier?
rephrase_cases.context: He dislikes apps, but a neighbor's scheduled Tuesday coffee works well.

conversation.content: What makes a community event workable for you?
If it finishes before dark and someone phones me about it, I am much more likely to go.
What makes a community event workable for you?
They're all the same.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: Can you think of one recent event you considered going to?

summary_conversation.content: What changed socially after retirement?
The daily workshop conversations disappeared. Some weeks I speak only to cashiers.
When does the week feel less empty?
My neighbor calls and we have coffee every Tuesday morning; having it fixed helps.

forbidden_claims: He is unable to learn apps

context.document: Retirement removed the repeated daily contact he had at the workshop.
He has skipped several interesting events because they ended after dark.
A fixed Tuesday morning coffee with a neighbor consistently creates meaningful contact.
Unscheduled intentions to call people are often postponed.

supported_patterns.mechanism: loss of structure removes automatic social contact
scheduled daytime contact fits his transport constraint

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Darius
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: Retirement removed routine social contact, while nighttime transport and app-based options are poor fits.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 67-year-old retiree who benefits from scheduled daytime contact and phone invitations.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Build recurring daytime, phone-coordinated social commitments around the successful Tuesday-coffee pattern.

persona.name: Priya
persona.context: Works rotating shifts and coordinates her mother's appointments.
constraints: cannot commit to the same daily time
fact_ledger: Appointment calls arrive during recovery sleep after night shifts.
She keeps tasks in several message threads and misses some.
A shared Sunday checklist worked twice but is not yet a pattern.
She wants fewer dropped tasks, not a perfect routine.

initial_problem: Everything keeps slipping through the cracks.

problem_framing.acceptable_followup: What kinds of things feel like they are slipping through the cracks right now?
problem_framing.clarification_answer: I work rotating hospital shifts and manage my mother's appointments. Messages and calls come while I should be sleeping, and I miss tasks or remember them too late.

rephrase_cases.original_question: Walk me through how a new appointment task enters your day.
rephrase_cases.context: The task-capture sequence is unknown.

rephrase_cases.original_question: Walk me through how a new appointment task enters your day.
rephrase_cases.context: She said her sister texts while she sleeps and she reads it on waking.

rephrase_cases.original_question: How does your schedule affect organization?
rephrase_cases.context: Day shifts are manageable; requests arriving during post-night-shift sleep are lost.

conversation.content: What happens to a task that arrives while you sleep?
I read the message half-awake, plan to add it later, and often forget after I get up.
What happens to a task that arrives while you sleep?
Not sure.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: Can you think of the most recent message that arrived while you were sleeping?

summary_conversation.content: How do caregiving tasks reach you?
They are split between my sister's texts, clinic calls, and a family group chat, often during recovery sleep.
What has helped at all?
We tried a shared Sunday checklist twice and it helped, but we have not made it regular.

forbidden_claims: The checklist is an established habit

context.document: Requests repeatedly arrive through three channels, so no single task list is complete.
Messages read during post-shift sleep are repeatedly forgotten before being recorded.
A shared Sunday checklist helped on two occasions, but recurrence is not established.
Day-shift weeks produce fewer missed tasks because she is awake when calls arrive.

supported_patterns.mechanism: fragmented intake plus half-awake reading loses tasks
task reliability changes with shift-related availability

forbidden_patterns: Sunday checklists always solve the problem

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Priya
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: Caregiving tasks are lost across channels and during recovery sleep around rotating shifts.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 44-year-old nurse managing her mother's appointments with limited backup.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Route requests into one low-friction capture point and process sleep-time messages at a shift-relative waking checkpoint rather than a fixed clock time.

persona.name: Noah
persona.context: Recently had one unusually difficult week after a schedule change.
fact_ledger: He was tired after one double shift.
He ordered takeout once.
He argued with a roommate once.
There is not enough repeated evidence for a pattern.

initial_problem: Last week was chaotic after my schedule changed, and I want to understand whether anything in my routine is making it worse.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What changed in last week's work schedule?
rephrase_cases.context: The schedule change is not described.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What changed in last week's work schedule?
rephrase_cases.context: He said he worked one double shift on Thursday.

rephrase_cases.original_question: How was work difficult?
rephrase_cases.context: Most shifts were normal; only Thursday was a double shift.

conversation.content: What changed in last week's schedule?
I covered one double shift on Thursday after a coworker called out.

validation_cases.reason: Specific usable context, despite being brief.

conversation.content: What changed in last week's schedule?
Stuff happened.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: What was different about one of your shifts last week?

summary_conversation.content: What was different last week?
A coworker called out, so I worked one double shift Thursday and slept poorly that night.
Has that happened on other weeks?
No, this was the first time in months.

context.document: He worked one double shift after a coworker called out.
He ordered takeout after that shift.
He slept poorly that Thursday night.
He reports that similar schedule disruption has not happened for months.

forbidden_patterns: Double shifts cause a recurring sleep-and-takeout loop

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Noah
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: A single chaotic week followed an unusual schedule disruption.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 31-year-old restaurant supervisor with only one week of relevant evidence.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Avoid strong conclusions; track future schedule disruptions before treating isolated events as patterns.

persona.name: Amina
persona.context: Uses her phone for customer messages and cannot simply switch it off.
fact_ledger: Nonurgent messages pull her into work after 10 p.m.
She stays up checking orders and wakes tired.
Using a separate urgent-contact ringtone helped several times.
She needs selective availability, not total disconnection.

initial_problem: I need my phone for the business, but checking customer messages at night keeps me awake and I am exhausted for school drop-off. I want a boundary that does not mean ignoring genuine emergencies.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What usually happens when a customer message arrives after 10 p.m.?
rephrase_cases.context: She has not described the response sequence.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What usually happens when a customer message arrives after 10 p.m.?
rephrase_cases.context: She said she opens it and then checks the full order dashboard.

rephrase_cases.original_question: How does your phone affect sleep?
rephrase_cases.context: Urgent calls are rare; nonurgent order messages trigger most late checking.

conversation.content: What happens after a nonurgent order message arrives?
I open the dashboard to check one thing and then start reviewing every open order.
What happens after a nonurgent order message arrives?
Phones are phones.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: What did you do the last time an order message arrived late?

summary_conversation.content: What happens with messages after 10?
A nonurgent order notification makes me open the dashboard, and I can stay there past midnight.
What has worked better?
I gave urgent customers a separate ringtone a few times; then I could mute ordinary alerts and still respond if needed.

context.document: Nonurgent order alerts repeatedly lead from one check to reviewing the whole dashboard.
Late dashboard sessions repeatedly delay sleep and make school drop-off exhausting.
On several nights, a distinct urgent-contact ringtone allowed ordinary alerts to stay muted.
True urgent messages are rare, but she needs to remain reachable for them.

supported_patterns.mechanism: ordinary alerts expand into work sessions and sleep loss
selective alerting preserves availability without all alerts

forbidden_patterns: She should turn off the phone

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Amina
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: Nonurgent business alerts expand into late work and sleep loss, but urgent availability is necessary.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 35-year-old business owner with early school drop-off and selective availability needs.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Separate urgent contacts from ordinary alerts, mute nonurgent notifications after 10 p.m., and defer dashboard review to a defined morning checkpoint.

persona.name: Leo
persona.context: Moved to a new city six weeks ago.
fact_ledger: He has sampled several unrelated activities once each.
He has not repeated any routine long enough to establish patterns.
He wants direction but lacks sufficient behavioral history.
Recommendations should focus on small experiments and observation.

initial_problem: I moved recently and feel like I should be building a life here, but I keep changing my mind about work, friends, and what to do with my days. I want some direction.

rephrase_cases.original_question: Tell me about the most recent choice that felt meaningful in the new city.
rephrase_cases.context: No meaningful choice has been described.

rephrase_cases.original_question: Tell me about the most recent choice that felt meaningful in the new city.
rephrase_cases.context: He attended one community kitchen event and enjoyed the practical work.

rephrase_cases.original_question: What goals interest you?
rephrase_cases.context: He is unsure about careers but repeatedly mentions wanting useful, hands-on work.

conversation.content: What kind of direction would feel useful right now?
I would like one practical project that lets me meet people without choosing a whole career yet.
What kind of direction would feel useful right now?
You know, direction.

validation_cases.acceptable_followup: What is one part of life here you would most like to feel clearer about?

summary_conversation.content: What have you tried since moving?
I went to one running group, one community kitchen shift, and one networking event.
What stood out?
The kitchen felt useful and natural, but one visit is not enough to know if it fits.

forbidden_claims: The kitchen is his new purpose

context.document: He attended one running group.
He completed one community kitchen shift and enjoyed feeling useful.
He attended one networking event and felt uncertain.
None of the activities has been repeated yet because he moved only six weeks ago.

forbidden_patterns: Hands-on volunteering is his stable purpose

legacy_evaluator_fields.Name: Leo
legacy_evaluator_fields.Problem: A recent move has left work, community, and daily direction unsettled without enough history to infer stable patterns.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Person Details: 26-year-old new resident who has tried several activities only once.
legacy_evaluator_fields.Ethnographic Solution: Run small repeated experiments and observe energy, connection, and follow-through before drawing conclusions about goals or patterns.
